name: Chapter 1: Relations and Functions
description: Types of relations, equivalence relations and classes, one-one and onto functions, composition, inverse, counting functions and relations, with exam-style problems.

cards.term: Define a relation R from A to B.
cards.definition: Any subset of A × B. If (a, b) ∈ R we write a R b. There need be no “meaning” connecting a and b

cards.term: Empty and universal relation on a set A?
cards.definition: Empty: R = φ (nothing is related). Universal: R = A × A (everything is related to everything). Both are “trivial” relations

cards.term: Example 1: on the students of a boys’ school, is “a is sister of b” empty or universal? And “heights differ by less than 3 m”?
cards.definition: No student has a sister in the school: empty. Every height difference is under 3 m: universal (A × A)

cards.term: Define reflexive, symmetric, transitive.
cards.definition:
Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R ∀ a.
Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R.
Transitive: (a, b), (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R

cards.term: What is an equivalence relation?
cards.definition: A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (all three)

cards.term: Reflexive, symmetric, transitive read from a digraph
cards.definition: Draw arrows a→b for (a,b) in R. Reflexive: a loop at every node. Symmetric: every arrow has a return arrow. Transitive: every two-step path a→b→c has the direct arrow a→c. Example 4: reflexive only

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Reading a relation as a graph

R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,3)} on {1, 2, 3}. Is it reflexive, symmetric, transitive?

Look for loops, return arrows and shortcuts.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Reading a relation as a graph

R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,3)} on {1, 2, 3}. Is it reflexive, symmetric, transitive?

Reflexive ✓ every element has a loop. Symmetric ✗: 1 → 2 has no return arrow 2 → 1. Transitive ✗: 1 → 2 → 3 needs the shortcut 1 → 3.

Test for each property: loops everywhere / every arrow returns / every two-step path has a shortcut.

cards.term: Trap: “symmetric and transitive, so it must be reflexive” (use (a,b),(b,a),(a,a)).
cards.definition: False. R = {(1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 1), (2, 2)} on {1, 2, 3} is symmetric and transitive but 3 is unrelated to itself: not reflexive. Every element of A must have (a, a)

cards.term: Which pairs decide transitivity?
cards.definition: Only chains: (a, b) and (b, c) both in R force (a, c). If there is no such chain the relation is vacuously transitive (e.g. R = {(1, 2)} is transitive, R = φ is symmetric and transitive)

cards.term: Example 3: L = lines in a plane, L₁ R L₂ iff L₁ ⟂ L₂. Which properties?
cards.definition: Symmetric only. Not reflexive (a line is not ⟂ itself); not transitive (L₁ ⟂ L₂ ⟂ L₃ gives L₁ ∥ L₃, so (L₁, L₃) ∉ R)

cards.term: Example 2: T₁ R T₂ iff T₁ is congruent to T₂ (triangles). Which properties?
cards.definition: Equivalence relation: congruent to itself if T₁ ≅ T₂ then T₂ ≅ T₁ T₁ ≅ T₂ ≅ T₃ gives T₁ ≅ T₃

cards.term: Example 5: R = {(a, b) : 2 divides a − b} on Z. Show it is an equivalence relation.
cards.definition: Reflexive: a − a = 0 is even. Symmetric: b − a = −(a − b) is even. Transitive: a − c = (a − b) + (b − c) is even. Equivalence ✓

cards.term: Equivalence classes of congruence mod 3
cards.definition: R = {(a,b): 3 | a−b} on Z is an equivalence relation with three classes [0], [1], [2] (remainders 0, 1, 2); they are disjoint and their union is Z

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Equivalence classes

R = {(a, b) : 3 divides a − b} on Z is an equivalence relation. Sort the integers into its equivalence classes.

Group numbers with the same remainder mod 3.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Equivalence classes

R = {(a, b) : 3 divides a − b} on Z is an equivalence relation. Sort the integers into its equivalence classes.

Three classes, by remainder on division by 3: [0] = {…, −3, 0, 3, 6, …}, [1] = {…, −2, 1, 4, 7, …}, [2] = {…, −4, −1, 2, 5, …}.

Classes are disjoint, their union is Z, and everything inside one class is related. Every equivalence relation partitions its set.

cards.term: What is an equivalence class [a]? What do the classes do to the set?
cards.definition: [a] = {b : (a, b) ∈ R}, all elements related to a. The classes are non-empty, mutually disjoint, and their union is the whole set: a partition. Conversely every partition gives an equivalence relation

cards.term: Example 5: the classes of “2 divides a − b” on Z?
cards.definition: [0] = even integers and [1] = odd integers. [0] = [2r], [1] = [2r + 1], [0] ≠ [1], and Z = E ∪ O with E ∩ O = φ

cards.term: Example 6: R = {(a, b) : a and b both odd or both even} on {1, ..., 7}. Its classes?
cards.definition: {1, 3, 5, 7} and {2, 4, 6}. Elements of one are related to each other, none related across

cards.term: Example 18: R₁, R₂ equivalence relations on A. Is R₁ ∩ R₂ an equivalence relation? R₁ ∪ R₂?
cards.definition: R₁ ∩ R₂ is (each property survives intersection). R₁ ∪ R₂ need not be: it can fail transitivity, e.g. R₁ = {1,2 together}, R₂ = {2,3 together} on {1,2,3} gives (1,2), (2,3) but not (1,3)

cards.term: Example 19: (x, y) R (u, v) iff xv = yu on pairs of positive integers. Equivalence? What is it saying?
cards.definition: Yes. It says x/y = u/v: two pairs are related when they are the same fraction. Transitivity: xv = yu and ub = va give x/y = u/v = a/b

cards.term: Example 21: f : X → Y, R = {(a, b) : f(a) = f(b)}. Type of relation?
cards.definition: Equivalence relation. Reflexive, symmetric, transitive all come from equality of values. Its classes are the fibres (preimages) f⁻¹(y)

cards.term: Example 20: R₁ = “x − y divisible by 3” on {1,...,9} equals R₂ = “x, y in the same one of {1,4,7}, {2,5,8}, {3,6,9}”. Why?
cards.definition: Each block is one residue class mod 3, so two numbers differ by a multiple of 3 exactly when they are in the same block: R₁ = R₂

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q1(i): R = {(x, y) : 3x − y = 0} on A = {1, ..., 14}. Reflexive, symmetric, transitive?
cards.definition: R = {(1,3), (2,6), (3,9), (4,12)}. (1, 1) ∉ R: not reflexive. (1, 3) ∈ R but (3, 1) ∉ R: not symmetric. (1,3), (3,9) ∈ R but (1, 9) ∉ R: not transitive. None of the three

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q1(ii): R = {(x, y) : y = x + 5 and x < 4} on N. Properties?
cards.definition: R = {(1,6), (2,7), (3,8)}. Not reflexive, not symmetric. No chain (b, c) starts from a second coordinate (6, 7, 8 are not first coordinates), so transitive holds vacuously: transitive only

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q1(iii): R = {(x, y) : y is divisible by x} on {1, ..., 6}. Properties?
cards.definition: x | x: reflexive. 2 | 4 but 4 ∤ 2: not symmetric. x | y and y | z ⇒ x | z: transitive. Reflexive and transitive, not symmetric

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q1(iv): R = {(x, y) : x − y is an integer} on Z. Properties?
cards.definition: x − y is always an integer, so R = Z × Z is the universal relation: equivalence relation

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q1(v)(a),(b): “work at the same place”, “live in the same locality”?
cards.definition: Both are equivalence relations: same-place / same-locality is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (the classes are the workplaces / localities)

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q1(v)(c): “x is exactly 7 cm taller than y”. Properties?
cards.definition: None: x is not 7 cm taller than x if x is 7 cm taller than y then y is not taller than x and x is 14 cm taller than z, not 7 cm

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q1(v)(d),(e): “x is wife of y” and “x is father of y”?
cards.definition: (d) not reflexive, not symmetric (y is not the wife of x), but transitive (vacuously). (e) neither reflexive, symmetric nor transitive (father of father is grandfather)

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q2: show R = {(a, b) : a ≤ b²} on R is neither reflexive, symmetric nor transitive.
cards.definition:
Reflexive fails: ½ ≤ ¼ is false, so (½, ½) ∉ R. Symmetric fails: (1, 4) ∈ R (1 ≤ 16) but (4, 1) ∉ R (4 ≤ 1 is false).
Transitive fails: (3, 2) ∈ R (3 ≤ 4) and (2, 1.5) ∈ R (2 ≤ 2.25) but (3, 1.5) ∉ R (3 ≤ 2.25 false)

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q3: R = {(a, b) : b = a + 1} on {1, ..., 6}. Properties?
Ex 1.1 Q4: R = {(a, b) : a ≤ b} on R. Properties?
cards.definition: Reflexive (a ≤ a), transitive (a ≤ b ≤ c ⇒ a ≤ c), not symmetric (1 ≤ 2 but 2 ≰ 1). This is a partial order, not an equivalence relation

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q5: R = {(a, b) : a ≤ b³} on R. Properties?
cards.definition: Not reflexive: ½ ≰ (½)³ = ⅛. Not symmetric: (1, 2) ∈ R but 2 ≰ 1. Not transitive: (10, 3): 10 ≤ 27, (3, 1.5): 3 ≤ 3.375, but 10 ≤ (1.5)³ = 3.375 is false. None of the three

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q6: R = {(1, 2), (2, 1)} on {1, 2, 3}. Show symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive.
cards.definition:
Symmetric: (1,2) and (2,1) both there.
Not reflexive: (1,1) ∉ R. Not transitive: (1,2), (2,1) ∈ R but (1,1) ∉ R

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q7: R = {(x, y) : x and y books with the same number of pages}. Show equivalence.
cards.definition: Same page count: reflexive, symmetric (equality is symmetric), transitive (equality is transitive). Equivalence ✓ (classes = books with a given page count)

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q8: R = {(a, b) : |a − b| is even} on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Equivalence? Classes?
cards.definition: Even difference ⇔ same parity, so equivalence. Classes {1, 3, 5} and {2, 4}: none related across (an odd and an even number differ by an odd number)

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q9: A = {0, ..., 12}. R = {(a, b) : |a − b| is a multiple of 4}. Elements related to 1?
cards.definition: Equivalence (same remainder mod 4). Need |1 − b| ∈ {0, 4, 8, 12}: {1, 5, 9}. For R = {(a, b) : a = b} only {1}

cards.term:
Ex 1.1 Q10: give an example of a relation on {1, 2, 3} that is
(i) symmetric not reflexive nor transitive
(ii) transitive not reflexive nor symmetric.
cards.definition:
(i) {(1,2), (2,1)}.
(ii) {(1,2)}: no chain, so vacuously transitive; not symmetric, not reflexive

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q10 (iii)–(v): reflexive+symmetric not transitive; reflexive+transitive not symmetric; symmetric+transitive not reflexive.
Ex 1.1 Q11: R = {(P, Q) : OP = OQ} for points of the plane. Class of P ≠ (0, 0)?
cards.definition: Same distance from the origin is an equivalence relation. The class of P is all points at distance OP: the circle through P with centre O

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q12: T₁ (3,4,5), T₂ (5,12,13), T₃ (6,8,10). Under “similar to”, which are related?
cards.definition: Similar triangles have proportional sides: 6:8:10 = 3:4:5, so T₁ and T₃ are related; T₂ is not

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q13: R = {(P₁, P₂) : same number of sides} on polygons. Class of the 3-4-5 triangle?
cards.definition: The set of all triangles (all polygons with 3 sides)

cards.term: Ex 1.1 Q14: R = {(L₁, L₂) : L₁ ∥ L₂} on lines in the XY plane. Lines related to y = 2x + 4?
cards.definition: Parallel ⇔ same slope 2: all lines y = 2x + c, c ∈ R

cards.term:
Ex 1.1 Q15: R = {(1,2), (2,2), (1,1), (4,4), (1,3), (3,3), (3,2)} on {1,2,3,4}. Choose:
(A) reflexive, symmetric not transitive
(B) reflexive, transitive not symmetric
(C) symmetric, transitive not reflexive
(D) equivalence
cards.definition: All four (a, a) present: reflexive. (1,2) ∈ R, (2,1) ∉ R: not symmetric. (1,3),(3,2) give (1,2) ✓: transitive. (B)
Need b > 6 and a = b − 2: (6, 8): 8 > 6 and 6 = 8 − 2 ✓. (2,4) and (3,8) fail a = b − 2 or b > 6; (8,7) fails. (C)

cards.term: Define one-one (injective).
cards.definition: f(x₁) = f(x₂) ⇒ x₁ = x₂ for all x₁, x₂. Distinct elements have distinct images; otherwise f is many-one

cards.term: Define onto (surjective).
cards.definition: Every y ∈ Y is f(x) for some x ∈ X, equivalently range = codomain

cards.term: Define bijective.
cards.definition: One-one and onto

cards.term: Why is “range = codomain” the same as onto?
cards.definition:
Range = the set of values actually hit; codomain = the set we declared.
If every codomain element is hit they are equal; if some element is missed, range ⊊ codomain

cards.term: Injective, surjective and bijective from arrow diagrams
cards.definition: One-one: no two arrows meet at one image; onto: every element of the codomain is hit. (a) one-one not onto; (b) neither; (c) onto not one-one; (d) bijective

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
One-one and onto · arrow diagrams

Classify each function (left → right): one-one? onto?

Look for shared targets and unused targets.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
One-one and onto · arrow diagrams

Classify each function (left → right): one-one? onto?

One-one (injective): no two arrows land on the same point (no orange dot). Onto (surjective): every right-hand point is hit (no red dot).

Bijective = both: a perfect pairing. Onto ⇔ range = codomain.

cards.term: How do you prove f is one-one? How do you prove it is onto?
cards.definition: One-one: assume f(x₁) = f(x₂) and derive x₁ = x₂. Onto: take any y in the codomain, solve y = f(x) for x, and check that x lies in the domain

cards.term: How do you disprove one-one? Disprove onto?
cards.definition: Not one-one: exhibit two different inputs with the same output (f(−1) = f(1)). Not onto: exhibit one codomain element with no input (−2 = x² has no real x)

cards.term: Horizontal line test for one-one and onto
cards.definition: Horizontal line test: one-one iff each horizontal line meets the graph at most once; onto R iff each meets it at least once. x² is neither; x³ is bijective

cards.term: Example 8: f : N → N, f(x) = 2x. One-one? Onto?
cards.definition: One-one (2x₁ = 2x₂ ⇒ x₁ = x₂), not onto: 1 = 2x has no natural solution (odd numbers are missed)

cards.term: Example 9: f : R → R, f(x) = 2x. One-one and onto?
cards.definition: Both. Given y ∈ R, x = y/2 ∈ R and f(y/2) = y. Same rule, bigger domain and codomain, now onto (compare Example 8)

cards.term: Trap: does a function’s rule alone decide one-one/onto?
cards.definition: No: the domain and codomain matter. f(x) = 2x is not onto N → N but is onto R → R; x² is not one-one on R but is one-one on [0, ∞)

cards.term: Example 10: f : N → N, f(1) = f(2) = 1, f(x) = x − 1 for x > 2. One-one? Onto?
cards.definition: Not one-one (f(1) = f(2) = 1). Onto: for y ≠ 1 take x = y + 1 (> 2), f(y + 1) = y; and f(1) = 1

cards.term: Example 11: f : R → R, f(x) = x². One-one? Onto?
cards.definition: Neither: f(−1) = f(1) = 1 and −2 is not a square

cards.term: Example 12: f(x) = x + 1 (x odd), x − 1 (x even), on N. Bijective?
cards.definition: Yes. It swaps 1 ↔ 2, 3 ↔ 4, 5 ↔ 6, …: an involution, so f(f(x)) = x and f is its own inverse. If f(x₁) = f(x₂) with x₁ odd, x₂ even then x₂ − x₁ = 2, impossible (odd and even differ by an odd number)

cards.term: Example 7: A = 50 students, f : A → N, f(x) = roll number. One-one? Onto?
cards.definition: One-one (roll numbers are distinct) but not onto N (51 is no student’s roll number)

cards.term: Examples 13 and 14: f : {1, 2, 3} → {1, 2, 3}. Onto ⇒ one-one? One-one ⇒ onto?
cards.definition: Both true for any finite set X and f : X → X. Not true for infinite sets: f(x) = 2x on N is one-one not onto; Example 10 is onto not one-one. This is the difference between finite and infinite

cards.term: Pigeonhole view: A and B finite, f : A → B one-one. What do you know about n(A), n(B)?
cards.definition: n(A) ≤ n(B). If f is onto then n(A) ≥ n(B); if bijective then n(A) = n(B)

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q1: f : R* → R*, f(x) = 1/x. One-one and onto? What if the domain is N (codomain R* as before)?
cards.definition: 1/x₁ = 1/x₂ ⇒ x₁ = x₂; and y ∈ R* has source 1/y ∈ R*: bijective. With domain N: still one-one but not onto (e.g. 2/3 has 3/2 ∉ N as a source)

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q2(i),(ii): f(x) = x² on N → N and Z → Z.
cards.definition: N → N: one-one, not onto (2 is not a perfect square). Z → Z: neither (f(−1) = f(1), and −1, 2 are not squares)

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q2(iii)–(v): f(x) = x² on R → R; x³ on N → N; x³ on Z → Z.
cards.definition: x² on R: neither. x³ on N: one-one, not onto (2 is not a cube). x³ on Z: one-one, not onto (2 is not a cube of an integer)

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q3: greatest integer function f(x) = [x] on R → R is neither one-one nor onto. Why?
cards.definition: f(1.2) = f(1.5) = 1: not one-one. Range = Z ⊊ R (e.g. 0.5 has no source): not onto

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q4: modulus f(x) = |x| on R → R. Why neither?
cards.definition: f(−2) = f(2) = 2: not one-one. Range = [0, ∞), so −1 is not attained: not onto

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q5: signum function on R → R. Why neither?
cards.definition: Values are only −1, 0, 1. f(2) = f(3) = 1: not one-one; range {−1, 0, 1} ≠ R: not onto
Distinct inputs 1, 2, 3 go to distinct outputs 4, 5, 6: one-one (not onto: 7 is missed)

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q7(i): f : R → R, f(x) = 3 − 4x. One-one? Onto?
cards.definition: f(x₁) = f(x₂) ⇒ −4x₁ = −4x₂ ⇒ x₁ = x₂. For y take x = (3 − y)/4. Bijective (any non-constant linear function R → R is)

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q7(ii): f : R → R, f(x) = 1 + x². One-one? Onto?
cards.definition: Neither: f(−1) = f(1) = 2; range [1, ∞) so 0 has no source

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q8: f : A × B → B × A, f(a, b) = (b, a). Bijective?
cards.definition: If (b₁, a₁) = (b₂, a₂) then a₁ = a₂, b₁ = b₂: one-one. Any (b, a) ∈ B × A is f(a, b): onto. Bijective (it is its own “swap” inverse)

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q9: f : N → N, f(n) = (n + 1)/2 for n odd, n/2 for n even. Bijective?
cards.definition: f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 1: not one-one, so not bijective (it is onto: every m has source 2m). Answer No

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q10: f : R − {3} → R − {1}, f(x) = (x − 2)/(x − 3). One-one and onto?
cards.definition: f(x₁) = f(x₂) ⇒ (x₁ − 2)(x₂ − 3) = (x₂ − 2)(x₁ − 3) ⇒ x₁ = x₂. Solving y = (x − 2)/(x − 3): x = (3y − 2)/(y − 1), defined for y ≠ 1. Yes, bijective

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q11: f : R → R, f(x) = x⁴. (A) one-one onto (B) many-one onto (C) one-one not onto (D) neither
cards.definition: f(−1) = f(1): not one-one. Range [0, ∞), −1 missed: not onto. (D)

cards.term: Ex 1.2 Q12: f : R → R, f(x) = 3x. (A) one-one onto (B) many-one onto (C) one-one not onto (D) neither
cards.definition: Linear with non-zero slope: (A) one-one and onto

cards.term: Define the composition gof.
cards.definition: f : A → B, g : B → C. Then gof : A → C, gof(x) = g(f(x)): f acts first, g second. Needs range of f ⊂ domain of g

cards.term: gof follows f then g
cards.definition: gof(x) = g(f(x)) apply f first; Example 15: gof(2)=7, gof(3)=7, gof(4)=11, gof(5)=11 (15 is not hit)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Composition of functions

f : {2,3,4,5} → {3,4,5,9} and g : {3,4,5,9} → {7,11,15} are given by the arrows. Find gof.

Follow each element through both arrow sets.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Composition of functions

f : {2,3,4,5} → {3,4,5,9} and g : {3,4,5,9} → {7,11,15} are given by the arrows. Find gof.

gof(x) = g(f(x)): apply f first, then g. Follow each element along blue then red.

gof(2) = g(3) = 7, gof(3) = g(4) = 7, gof(4) = g(5) = 11, gof(5) = g(5) = 11. So gof = {(2,7), (3,7), (4,11), (5,11)}.

cards.term: Example 16: f(x) = cos x, g(x) = 3x². Find gof and fog. Are they equal?
cards.definition: gof(x) = g(cos x) = 3 cos²x; fog(x) = f(3x²) = cos 3x². At x = 0: gof = 3 but fog = 1. gof ≠ fog

cards.term: Is composition commutative? associative?
cards.definition: Not commutative (gof ≠ fog in general). Associative: (hog)of = ho(gof). f o I = I o f = f for the identity

cards.term: Compose: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Find gof(3), fog(3).
cards.definition: f(3) = 7, gof(3) = g(7) = 49. g(3) = 9, fog(3) = f(9) = 19

cards.term: If f is one-one and g is one-one, is gof one-one? If both onto?
cards.definition: Yes in both cases. And if gof is one-one then f is one-one; if gof is onto then g is onto (the outer/inner function that must “carry” the property)

cards.term: Definition of invertible function.
cards.definition: f : X → Y is invertible if ∃ g : Y → X with gof = I_X and fog = I_Y. Then g = f⁻¹

cards.term: Which functions are invertible?
cards.definition: Exactly the bijections (one-one and onto). One-one makes the inverse single-valued, onto makes it defined on all of Y

cards.term: Graph of f⁻¹ is the mirror image of f in y = x
cards.definition: f⁻¹ swaps (a,b) to (b,a): the graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in y = x; only bijections are invertible; for f(x)=x³, f⁻¹(x)=cube root of x

cards.term: Example 17: f : N → Y, f(x) = 4x + 3, Y = {4x + 3 : x ∈ N}. Show invertible and find the inverse.
cards.definition: f is one-one and onto Y. From y = 4x + 3: x = (y − 3)/4. So g(y) = (y − 3)/4. Check: g(f(x)) = (4x + 3 − 3)/4 = x and f(g(y)) = 4(y − 3)/4 + 3 = y

cards.term: Method: find f⁻¹ of a bijection.
cards.definition:
1) Write y = f(x).
2) Solve for x in terms of y.
3) Swap names: f⁻¹(x) = that expression.
4) Check f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.
The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f

cards.term: Find the inverse of f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) (x ≠ 3).
cards.definition: y(x − 3) = 2x + 1 → x(y − 2) = 3y + 1 → f⁻¹(x) = (3x + 1)/(x − 2) (x ≠ 2). Note f⁻¹ has the same form, with the roles of the numbers rearranged

cards.term: If f and g are invertible, what is (gof)⁻¹?
cards.definition: f⁻¹ o g⁻¹ (socks and shoes: undo the last step first)

cards.term: Trap: is f⁻¹(x) the same as 1/f(x)?
cards.definition: No. f⁻¹ is the inverse function (undoes f). 1/f(x) is the reciprocal. For f(x) = 2x: f⁻¹(x) = x/2 but 1/f(x) = 1/(2x)

cards.term: When is f = f⁻¹ (an involution)?
cards.definition:
When f(f(x)) = x.
Examples: f(x) = 1/x, f(x) = −x + c, and Example 12 (swapping 1 ↔ 2, 3 ↔ 4, …).
The graph is symmetric about y = x

cards.term: Domain restriction: f(x) = x² is not invertible on R. How to make it invertible?
cards.definition: Restrict to [0, ∞) → [0, ∞): now one-one and onto, with inverse √x. Restricting to (−∞, 0] gives the inverse −√x

cards.term: Example 22: number of one-one functions from {1, 2, 3} to itself?
cards.definition: Each is a permutation of 3 symbols: 3! = 6. In general n! for a set of n elements (Misc Q4)

cards.term: Example 23: A = {1,2,3}. How many relations contain (1,2) and (2,3) and are reflexive and transitive but not symmetric?
cards.definition: Forced: the diagonal, (1,2), (2,3) and, by transitivity, (1,3). That is R₁. Add (2,1) alone: still transitive, not symmetric. Add (3,2) alone: same. Adding (3,1), or two of the missing pairs, forces every pair and the relation becomes symmetric. So 3: R₁, R₁ ∪ {(2,1)}, R₁ ∪ {(3,2)}

cards.term: Example 24: number of equivalence relations on {1, 2, 3} containing (1, 2) and (2, 1)?
cards.definition: Smallest: {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1)} (classes {1,2}, {3}). Relating 3 to either forces everything (universal). 2

cards.term: Example 25: I_N is onto. Is I_N + I_N (x ↦ 2x) onto N → N?
cards.definition: No: 3 ∈ N has no natural x with 2x = 3. Sum of onto functions need not be onto

cards.term: Example 26: f = sin, g = cos on [0, π/2]. One-one? Is f + g one-one?
cards.definition: sin and cos are each strictly monotone there: one-one. But (f + g)(0) = 1 = (f + g)(π/2), so f + g is not one-one

cards.term: Misc Q1: f : R → (−1, 1), f(x) = x/(1 + |x|). One-one and onto?
cards.definition: For x ≥ 0, f = x/(1 + x) ∈ [0, 1); for x < 0, f = x/(1 − x) ∈ (−1, 0). Solving y = x/(1 + |x|): x = y/(1 − |y|). Bijective (a stretched “S-curve” squeezing R into (−1, 1))

cards.term: Misc Q2: f : R → R, f(x) = x³ is injective. Proof?
cards.definition: x₁³ = x₂³ ⇒ (x₁ − x₂)(x₁² + x₁x₂ + x₂²) = 0. The second factor is > 0 unless both are 0, so x₁ = x₂

cards.term: Misc Q3: on P(X), ARB iff A ⊂ B. Equivalence relation?
cards.definition: Reflexive ✓ (A ⊂ A), transitive ✓, but not symmetric: {1} ⊂ {1, 2} but {1, 2} ⊄ {1}. No (it is a partial order)

cards.term: Misc Q4: number of onto functions from {1, 2, ..., n} to itself?
cards.definition: For a finite set onto ⇔ one-one ⇔ permutation: n!
f: 2, 0, 0, 2 at −1, 0, 1, 2. g: 2·1.5 − 1 = 2, 0, 0, 2. Equal: same domain, same codomain, same value at every point

cards.term:
Misc Q6: A = {1,2,3}. Relations containing (1,2) and (1,3), reflexive and symmetric, not transitive:
(A) 1
(B) 2
(C) 3
(D) 4
cards.definition: Forced: diagonal plus (1,2), (2,1), (1,3), (3,1). Missing (2,3), (3,2): adding one alone breaks symmetry, adding both makes it universal (transitive). So exactly (A) 1

cards.term:
Misc Q7: A = {1,2,3}. Equivalence relations containing (1, 2):
(A) 1
(B) 2
(C) 3
(D) 4
cards.definition: Partitions with 1 and 2 together: {1,2}{3} and {1,2,3}. (B) 2

cards.term: Two equal functions: what must match?
cards.definition: Same domain, same codomain and f(x) = g(x) for every x in the domain (Misc Q5). f(x) = x on R and f(x) = √(x²) are different functions

cards.term: n(A) = m, n(B) = n. Number of functions A → B?
cards.definition: nᵐ: each of the m inputs chooses one of n outputs

cards.term: n(A) = m, n(B) = n. Number of one-one functions A → B?
cards.definition: ⁿPₘ = n(n − 1)···(n − m + 1) (0 if m > n). Example: from {1,2,3} to a 5-set: 5·4·3 = 60

cards.term: Number of onto functions from an m-set onto an n-set?
cards.definition: Inclusion–exclusion: Σₖ (−1)ᵏ ⁿCₖ (n − k)ᵐ. Two useful cases: onto from an m-set to a 2-set is 2ᵐ − 2; onto from a 4-set to a 3-set is 36

cards.term: Number of bijections from an n-set to itself?
cards.definition: n!

cards.term: Number of relations from A to B and on A (n(A) = n)?
cards.definition: A → B: 2^(mn) (subsets of A × B). On A: 2^(n²)

cards.term: Number of reflexive relations on an n-set? Of symmetric ones?
cards.definition: Reflexive: diagonal forced, other n² − n pairs free: 2^(n² − n). Symmetric: choose each unordered pair and each loop: 2^(n(n+1)/2). For n = 3 both are 64

cards.term: Number of reflexive AND symmetric relations on an n-set?
cards.definition: 2^(n(n − 1)/2) (only the off-diagonal unordered pairs are free). n = 3: 8

cards.term: Number of equivalence relations on sets of size 1, 2, 3, 4, 5?
cards.definition: Number of partitions (Bell numbers): 1, 2, 5, 15, 52

cards.term: Number of equivalence relations on {1, 2, 3, 4} containing (1, 2)?
cards.definition: Partitions of {1,2,3,4} where 1 and 2 are together = partitions of {12, 3, 4} = 5

cards.term: Number of symmetric relations on {1, 2, 3} containing (1, 2)?
cards.definition: Free unordered pairs/loops: 6 in total, one fixed: 2⁵ = 32

cards.term: f : A → B is one-one with n(A) = 4 and n(B) = 3. Possible?
cards.definition: No: one-one needs n(A) ≤ n(B) (pigeonhole). Six or more distinct outputs would be needed

cards.term: f : {1, 2, 3} → {a, b, c}. How many are neither one-one nor onto?
cards.definition: Total 27 bijections 6 for finite equal sets onto ⇔ one-one, so neither = 27 − 6 = 21

cards.term:
MCQ: R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,1)} on {1,2,3} is
(a) reflexive only (b) symmetric only (c) transitive only (d) equivalence
cards.definition: Reflexive ✓ symmetric ✓ transitive: (1,2),(2,1) ⇒ (1,1) ✓ (2,1),(1,2) ⇒ (2,2) ✓. (d) equivalence

cards.term:
MCQ: R = {(a, b) : a ≤ b} on R is
(a) equivalence (b) reflexive and transitive only (c) symmetric only (d) none
cards.definition: (b): partial order

cards.term:
MCQ: on Z, R = {(a, b) : a − b is divisible by 5}. Number of equivalence classes?
(a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 4 (d) 5
cards.definition: One class per remainder 0–4: (d) 5

cards.term:
MCQ: f : R → R, f(x) = x|x| is
(a) one-one, not onto (b) onto, not one-one (c) bijective (d) neither
cards.definition: Increasing (−x² for x < 0, x² for x ≥ 0), and every real is attained: (c) bijective

cards.term:
MCQ: f : R → R, f(x) = sin x is
(a) one-one (b) onto (c) both (d) neither
cards.definition: sin(0) = sin(π), range [−1, 1] ≠ R: (d) neither

cards.term:
MCQ: f : R → R, f(x) = x³ + x. Then f is
(a) one-one, not onto (b) many-one (c) bijective (d) neither
cards.definition: Strictly increasing (f′ = 3x² + 1 > 0) and cubic (goes to ±∞): (c) bijective

cards.term:
MCQ: f : [0, ∞) → [0, ∞), f(x) = x². f is
(a) one-one not onto (b) onto not one-one (c) bijective (d) neither
cards.definition: (c). Compare f : R → R, where it is neither
g(2) = 4, f(4) = 11: (a) 11
y = 5x − 3 → x = (y + 3)/5: (a)

cards.term:
MCQ: number of one-one functions from {1, 2, 3} to {a, b, c, d, e} is
(a) 15 (b) 60 (c) 125 (d) 243
cards.definition: 5 × 4 × 3 = (b) 60

cards.term:
MCQ: number of onto functions from {1, 2, 3, 4} to {a, b, c} is
(a) 36 (b) 81 (c) 24 (d) 12
cards.definition: 3⁴ − 3·2⁴ + 3 = 81 − 48 + 3 = (a) 36

cards.term:
MCQ: number of reflexive relations on a set with 3 elements is
(a) 8 (b) 64 (c) 512 (d) 9
cards.definition: 2^(9 − 3) = (b) 64

cards.term: Integer answer (JEE Main): number of equivalence relations on {a, b, c, d} containing (a, b)?
cards.definition: Partitions of {ab, c, d} = 5

cards.term: Integer answer: n(A) = 3, n(B) = 4. Number of one-one functions A → B?
cards.definition: 4 · 3 · 2 = 24

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: f : R → R, f(x) = x² is not invertible.
R: f is not one-one.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true
cards.definition: (a): invertible ⇔ bijective; f(−1) = f(1) shows f is not one-one (and also not onto)

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: A relation on {1, 2, 3} that is symmetric and transitive is reflexive.
R: (a, b) and (b, a) give (a, a).
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) A false, R true (c) A true, R false (d) Both false
cards.definition: (b): R is true only for elements that appear in some pair; an isolated element (like 3 in {(1,2),(2,1),(1,1),(2,2)}) breaks A

cards.term: True/False: every reflexive relation on a set with two or more elements is symmetric.
cards.definition: False: {(1,1), (2,2), (1,2)} is reflexive but not symmetric

cards.term: True/False: if f : A → B is onto and A, B are finite with n(A) = n(B), then f is one-one.
cards.definition: True: finite sets, same size: onto ⇔ one-one

cards.term: 2-mark: check whether R = {(x, y) : x + y = 6} on {1, ..., 5} is reflexive, symmetric or transitive.
cards.definition: R = {(1,5), (2,4), (3,3), (4,2), (5,1)}. Not reflexive ((1,1) ∉ R). Symmetric (x + y = y + x). Not transitive: (1,5), (5,1) ∈ R but (1,1) ∉ R

cards.term: 3-mark: show that f : R → R, f(x) = (2x − 1)/3 is bijective and find f⁻¹.
cards.definition: f(x₁) = f(x₂) ⇒ x₁ = x₂ (one-one). For y take x = (3y + 1)/2 (onto). f⁻¹(x) = (3x + 1)/2

cards.term: 3-mark: f(x) = x + 5 on Z. Show that f is invertible; find f⁻¹.
cards.definition: One-one (x₁ + 5 = x₂ + 5), onto (y − 5 ∈ Z is a source). f⁻¹(y) = y − 5

cards.term: 4-mark: show that R = {(a, b) : a − b is divisible by 3} on Z is an equivalence relation. Find [1].
cards.definition: Reflexive (0), symmetric (negation), transitive (sum). [1] = {…, −5, −2, 1, 4, 7, …} = {3r + 1}

cards.term: 4-mark: show that f : R → R, f(x) = x² + 1 is neither one-one nor onto. Restrict the domain and codomain to make it a bijection.
cards.definition: f(−1) = f(1) = 2 and 0 ∉ range. Take f : [0, ∞) → [1, ∞): one-one (x ≥ 0) and onto ([1, ∞) is exactly the range), with f⁻¹(y) = √(y − 1)

cards.term: Case-based: the relation “sits in the same bench” on the students of a class (each student sits on exactly one bench). What type of relation is it? What are its equivalence classes?
cards.definition: Equivalence relation (each student is on the same bench as themselves; symmetric; transitive). The classes are the benches (groups of students on the same bench)

cards.term: Case-based: a school assigns each student in a class a roll number, f(x) = roll number, A = 40 students, codomain N. One-one? Onto? Make it a bijection.
cards.definition: One-one (no two share a roll number), not onto N. Restrict the codomain to {1, …, 40}: then f is a bijection and invertible
